q-162545.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14231848/assets/1cac5607abe416bf2ba5b4a6af42315edcc898034331034de68dd4c9be151c5e.png)

What is the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,j$ across the curve $C$ shown above?

*Hint: Start by checking whether $F$ is source-free.*
q-162545.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,ds$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,ds={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,ds.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =0+0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $F$ is a source-free vector field. So, the flux of $F$ across any closed curve is zero.
Hence,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,ds=0.
$$

What is the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j$ across the curve $C$ shown above?

*Hint: Start by checking whether $F$ is source-free.*
q-162549.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡y \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $F$ is *not* a source-free vector field. 

Since $F$ is not source-free, we do not have enough information to determine the flux of $F$ through $C.$

q-162555.name: Question 3
q-162555.problem:
Given the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+2xy\,j,$ which of the following statements must be true?

I. $∇\cdot F\ne 0$

II. There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F$

III. $F$ is a source-free vector field
q-162555.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

Note that $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+2xy\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)={x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=2xy.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each statement.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+2x=4x\ne 0.
$$

- Statements II and III are false. Indeed, this follows from statement I.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

q-162628.name: Question 4
q-162628.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14231848/assets/84cfc63faa3514c7b6151d5ab8f3f8e4e7deaafa8739fa637af2f0ce7453b7fb.png)

The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(1,1)$ and $B(5,4).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i-2xy\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free.*
q-162628.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy)=2x-2x=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,1)$ to $B(5,4)$ and  ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14231848/assets/18b1a5bdc11ca3c2b4b728cf8df3a3e1c4b6c2fbbe86549e9ad773367495c533.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+j+t\cdot [(5\,i+4j)-(i+j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+(3t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=(4t+1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}+8t+1, \\ Q(x,y) & =-2xy=-2(4t+1)(3t+1)=-24{t}^{2}-14t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+1)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((16{t}^{2}+8t+1)\cdot (3)-(-24{t}^{2}-14t-2)\cdot (4))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,144{t}^{2}+80t+11\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[48{t}^{3}+40{t}^{2}+11t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(48+40+11) \\  & =99.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=99.
$$

The curve C1 has endpoints A(1,1) and B(5,4). Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=x2i−2xyj through C1 measured with respect to the unit normal vector n1, as shown above.

Hint: You're given that F is source-free.

a
80
b
81
c
100
d
99
e
90
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field with simply connected domain D⊆R2, then the following are equivalent:

  • F is a source-free vector field.

  • ∇⋅F=∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=0.

  • The flux ∮CF⋅nds along any closed curve C∈D is zero.

  • Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves C1,C2∈D with the same start and endpoints, we have that ∫C1F⋅nds=∫C2F⋅nds.

  • There exists a stream function ψ(x,y) for F.

First, notice that

∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=∂∂x(x2)+∂∂y(−2xy)=2x−2x=0,

which shows that F is a source-free vector field.

Since F is source-free, we know the flux of F is independent of the path. In particular,

∫C1F⋅n1ds=∫C2F⋅n2ds,

where C2 is the straight line from A(1,1) to B(5,4) and n2 is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

Notice that both n1 and n2 are 90∘ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of F across C2, we will use the formula

∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2Pdy−Qdx.

To apply the formula,

  • the curve should be parametrized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n2 must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector T(t).

Parametrizing C2, we have

r(t)=i+j+t⋅[(5i+4j)−(i+j)]=(4t+1)i+(3t+1)j

where t∈[0,1]. Therefore,

P(x,y)=x2=(4t+1)2=16t2+8t+1,Q(x,y)=−2xy=−2(4t+1)(3t+1)=−24t2−14t−2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(4t+1)=4,dydt=ddt(3t+1)=3.

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2Pdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01((16t2+8t+1)⋅(3)−(−24t2−14t−2)⋅(4))dt=∫01(144t2+80t+11)dt=[48t3+40t2+11t]01=(48+40+11)=99.

Finally, we conclude that

∫C1F⋅n1ds=99.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{{y}^{3}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2})=0+0=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,3)$ to $B(5,3)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14231848/assets/3d64ffb0e4cc313a2857d1c20922c1202619d0bdeb3d97f2808b4995c99f7f9f.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+3\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+3\,j)-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=-\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=-\sqrt{27}, \\ Q(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}=((4t+1)-1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\sqrt{27})\cdot (0)-(16{t}^{2})\cdot (4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-64{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{64{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-\frac{64}{3}.
$$

Question 5
?

The curve C1 has endpoints A(1,3) and B(5,3). Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=−y3i+(x−1)2j through C1 measured with respect to the unit normal vector n1, as shown above.

Hint: You're given that F is source-free.

a
−763
b
−643
c
−24
d
−283
e
−18
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field with simply connected domain D⊆R2, then the following are equivalent:

  • F is a source-free vector field.

  • ∇⋅F=∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=0.

  • The flux ∮CF⋅nds along any closed curve C∈D is zero.

  • Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves C1,C2∈D with the same start and endpoints, we have that ∫C1F⋅nds=∫C2F⋅nds.

  • There exists a stream function ψ(x,y) for F.

First, notice that

∂P∂x+∂Q∂y=∂∂x(−y3)+∂∂y((x−1)2)=0+0=0,

which shows that F is a source-free vector field.

Since F is source-free, we know the flux of F is independent of the path. In particular,

∫C1F⋅n1ds=∫C2F⋅n2ds,

where C2 is the straight line from A(1,3) to B(5,3) and n2 is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

Notice that both n1 and n2 are 90∘ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of F across C2, we will use the formula

∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2Pdy−Qdx.

To apply the formula,

  • the curve should be parametrized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n2 must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector T(t).

Parametrizing C2, we have

r(t)=i+3j+t⋅[(5i+3j)−(i+3j)]=(4t+1)i+3j

where t∈[0,1]. Therefore,

P(x,y)=−y3=−(3)3=−27,Q(x,y)=(x−1)2=((4t+1)−1)2=16t2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(4t+1)=4,dydt=ddt(3)=0.

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2Pdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01(−27)⋅(0)−(16t2)⋅(4)dt=∫01−64t2dt=[−64t33]01=−643.

Finally, we conclude that

∫C1F⋅n1ds=−643.
